texto:
Quasar's EP is excellent doom, and the song they have on here, "Parade of Planets," is of the same style of funeral doom

"Parade of Planets" has my favorite moments of funeral doom, but ultimately the worse organization of the Quasar material that I have heard.  The clean guitar interludes are utterly dazzling and beautfiul, and the synth parts are even more well constructed.  Vocals are much, much better than on the EP, because they seem more organic and human, and don't drown out the other instruments.  Guitars and drums are a merciless onslaught of brutal, frozen molasses ooze.  Rich and depressive.

The major downside is that it seems like the parts were just thrown together.  There are no strong segues.  There is an excellent clean guitar part with either some chick wailing over it or some eerie keyboard (I'm unsure which), followed by a swelling synth part.  The problem is, you can tell and feel quite well that these parts have absolutely nothing to do with one another.  It's a real shame, because the thing I love about slow music is that it morphs from one movement to another.  But on here, it doesn't, so I can't give it as high of a mark as the EP.

"Deeds, not words" is the title of British BM band Deitus' debut album, though without very much information about these guys at my finger-tips I can't say how much they live up to that motto. This is straightforward no-frills / no-nonsense 1990s-styled raw BM that stresses hard-edged martial riffing, outbreaks of blast-beat drumming and plenty of melodies in songs with occult and Satanic themes. All songs show thought and care in their construction and each track stands as a flowing self-contained unit in its own right with a lot of drama, aggression and energy. The weakest element here is the spidery BM vocals which are all but swamped by the energetic music, which is a bit unfortunate as most songs feature singing and the music accommodates it, never fighting it. While the guitars have a distorted sound, the band's overall style is actually clean and polished enough for all instruments to be heard clearly and the general sound is more steely and spacious than grinding.

All songs are played well and consistently though if they had fewer and more distinctive riffs and melodies they might all emerge as potential singles. Trying to pack in as many riffs as possible into each and every song has the unfortunate effect of robbing them all of their own identities. As they are, the longer tracks "Ladder of Divine Ascent" and "Todestrieb" coming at the end of the album stick out more, probably because they also feature some lead guitar playing, pay more attention to creating mood and ambience than the other earlier pieces or experiment a bit with the band's style and sound.

While the album is technically good and these Deitus guys have considerable ability and song-writing skills, they need to develop a more distinctive style and sound. At present they sound very much like 1,001 other generic raw black metal bands drawing on 1990s black metal influences and inspirations. The vocals very definitely need to improve beyond raspy spider chant and incorporating a second vocalist (with perhaps some death metal influence) probably wouldn't go astray. There are indications on the later tracks, especially "Todestrieb", that suggest that what I'm hearing here is just a small part of what Deitus are capable of and they could certainly incorporate more ambience and non-BM elements than they do here. 

C'mon guys, we're looking forward to your second album where deeds not words are what we want you to live up to!

I had been completely charmed by Category VI's debut record a few years back, so I was pleased for the chance to write about their sophomore effort. If you've yet to hear the band, then we're looking at some prime U.S. power metal with an old school slant.

"Strike of the Axe" delivers unto us Category VI's brand of metal circa 2017, with a godly guitar tone breaking through some atmospheric foreshadowing for a fist-banging anthem. Amanda Gosse's vocals command the punchy arrangements contained with a powerful, reverb kissed below, which absolutely does the job. I love the crooning adorning "Full Metal Jacket", giving me some sweet nostalgic vibes, though I can't pinpoint on what it may remind of. Nonetheless the vocals are a highlight throughout, and I'd say a step up from Fireborn.

Musically this is for the most part blazing, and performed in stellar fashion. There's plenty of riffs to sink your teeth into, complete with tasteful battery, and some raunchy bass lines although on the subject of bass I did feel some of the more flamboyant, effect-powered parts to be detrimental. but give me out their bass over inaudible bass any day. Rippers like "Mirror" and the aforementioned "Full Metal Jacket" outclass anything on the last album, so I'd say Category VI succeeded in writing a superior follow up.

If you dig acts like Seven Kingdoms, Mindmaze, or Helion Prime, then I'd call this a no brainer although Category VI do separate themselves from their contemporaries with a more pugilistic edge, and a lethal injection of classic metal attitude which would call to mind Judas Priest or Mercyful Fate. Overall a solid record. You could do far worse than check this out.

Written for The Metal Crypt

Among the many ways that the 2010s crop of traditional metal revivalists mirrored their NWOBHM inspirations was a sizable collection of projects with a lot of potential that just didn't end up going much of anywhere. The only noteworthy difference seems to be the various countries that have produced these undiscovered studio gems, as the scarcity of metal behind the iron curtain left little opportunity for aspiring bands to be crowded out of the scene. Nevertheless, the advent of the internet and various social media accounts focused exclusively on promoting various metal subgenres has afforded even the most obscure of outfits the opportunity to reach an audience, though even in this more advantageous disposition an outfit like Polish heavy metal upstarts Savager seemed destined from humble returns when their 2017 debut EP Casus Belli finally became available on cassette.

But for what this quintet may have lacked in notoriety during their brief run in the late 2010s, they all but made up for in iron grit and sheer determination, at least insofar as what they managed to commit to recording. In the same tradition inherited from the likes of Manilla Road, Manowar and Cirith Ungol, then transmitted to faithful adherents like Ironsword and Eternal Champion, Savager dabbles in low-fi, blood and guts territory that is not for the faint of heart nor the operatic Prima Donna. Tempos tend towards the swift side and flirt heavily with speed and thrash metal stylings, the visual of steel clad barbarians cutting their foes limb from limb and spilling blood upon some snow-covered battle field hangs in the listener's head. Yet while the resulting battery of rage constructed by this outfit's instrumentalists is truly impressive, the berserker growl and Eric Adams-like falcon cries of lead vocalist Bartek Koniuszewski is what ultimately sells this EP.

The auditory carnage arrives with no need of an elaborate introduction with a double kick-steeped, driving speed anthem right out of the early 80s Manowar example, spearheaded by a thunderous riff set and a bear-like roar from Bartek that culminates in the most off the hook offering of the pack. That being said, the similarly forceful and speedy sonic assault of "Evil" and the nimble riff work of the quick paced "Might Of The Thunder God" are similarly primed to leave an entire regiment of decapitated bodies in their respective wakes, the latter seeing some rock solid, Ross The Boss-inspired lead guitar passages to bring it all home. The instrumental romp "Leviathan" turns the tables towards more of a pummeling Omen vibe meets Iron Maiden's "Transylvania" for an interesting contrast point. But the most compelling contrast point amid all the speed and fury is the down tempo metallic stomp of "Call Of The Savage", channeling that more epic side of the Manowar coin, only minus the bloated interlude segments and voice overs.

On paper, this 20 minute slab of old school heavy metal in a comparably analog-like production package had all the right elements to be a major contender in the still bustling NWOTHM craze circa 2017. Sadly, little came of this apart from a few thousand listens on YouTube and 50 hand numbered cassette copies being dispersed to the four winds. It was almost to be expected given the large number of outfits still active and sporting this same exact sound, be it the aforementioned Ironsword and Eternal Champion, or the dozens of other lesser known projects spread about Europe and the Americas. It doesn't really push the envelope as hard as the aforementioned outfits, nor does go too far beyond the stylistic norms that go with an early 80s epic approach, but it's not without a clear sense of charm and is definitely worth a spin by any self-respecting true metal trustee.

Together since 2020 when they put out their debut release ""Zagovor" ("Charm"), Russian trio Ikotka have been busy refining their style of raw occult atmospheric black metal with several EP releases and two more albums. "Raspad" ("Disintegration" or "Decay") is the band's third album and, if you don't count a compilation and two singles, ninth release. As with earlier releases, "Raspad" revolves around the musicians' interest in protective charms and spells, this time to protect against the decay and disintegration of a past world of war and chaos and the damage this world is doing to them physically and psychologically. The lyrics of four of the five songs on the album are based on old Russian spells.

Once out of its starting gates, the album charges ahead like an angry wounded bull with an extremely raw and noisy guitar sound and thudding percussion, topped by harsh stentorian vocals that almost sound like throat singing and which enhance the majesty of the music in opening track "Немирье (Притча)" ("Wartime (Parable)"). The tremolo guitars exert a hypnotic effect in their metallic judder and the voices command attention with lyrics of the penetration of the evil of conflict and war into one's soul. The second track is just as harsh and severe in its style as the first track, though slower and brooding in parts. The melodies can be very stirring in their gloom and melancholy, strange though that might seem, but there is an aggressive force from within the musicians that is driving the music onwards and infusing it with power and a vision of where to go and how.

The songs might appear similar on first listen, but repeated spins reveal differences among the five tracks, with each one having a different mood and outlook than the others. The tracks trace a journey from a place of relative light in a mostly dark world into levels of greater darkness and sadness, with all the risks of torment and possible derangement that might go with them. The third track has a sense of tragic grandeur in its riffs and pounding drums. 

Track 4, "Оттерпеться от Пытки (Покаяние)" ("Stop Endure the Torment (Repentance)") starts out as a meditative drone ambient that steadily works itself into blasting melodic BM with clear and distinct lead guitar riffs in later parts of the long track. Compared to the previous tracks, this one is even more sombre and sorrowful in its aggression, even as the riffs ring out loudly and clearly. A surprising slow solo guitar passage suggesting inner mental torment and sadness comes near the end of the song. The final track, also the title track, has a triumphal air as the musicians complete the occult ritual and escape the fate of the damned.

Though Ikotka's sound is very raw and noisy, at the same time the music is clear enough that riffs and melodies can be heard and the moods they bring can be felt and absorbed by listeners. The trio play with a limited instrumental set-up – guitars, bass, percussion, synthesisers – but deliver a powerful and sometimes droning doom style of raw BM. That the songs trace a narrative through the changing moods of the music and the lyrics demonstrates the thought and care the musicians took in recording and presenting the songs in the order they appear. Though some tracks could have been edited for length and tightened up a little so that the music could have been even more forceful, there's hardly any filler on the recording. Every moment on the album has feeling, force and power. 

When it all ends, as it must, you have been swept up so much in the album's embrace that you can feel rather lost and alone, especially after that last track which has built up to a mighty sonic tower of raw tremolo-guitar noise and droning lead guitar.

The band idea takes its origins away back in 1997, when the guitar player Alessandro Pace, former member of avant-garde rock group Klimt 1918, thought of creating different music. Sadly, The Foreshadowing was formed only in 2005, when Alessandro found perfect band members for all of the instruments. Honestly, i didn't expect much from this album. Italian gothic based metal usually is full of Über-Mega-Cheesy moments. Macbeth, Mandragora Scream, Lacuna Coil or Theatres des Vampires could be considered "masters"...

This album contains none! It's also very solid, all tracks "touch" you emotionally and the riffs are rarely repeated, so getting bored while listening isn't possible. There are many powerful moments in the songs that give you feelings of melancholy that only expressive music like Anathema's "Angelica", "Far Away" or "Fragile Dreams" can create. You are probably guessing the album is gothic metal, but the almost omnipresent irksome-doomy guitar work and almost omnipresent depressing keyboard makes it gothic-doom metal. The emotional "Anathema" moments are usually obtained when the lead guitar becomes more melodic and the keyboard gets more intense, but it's important to say that nothing would be possible without Marco Benevento's incredibly soothing baritone (the only type of vocals on DoN). Such flavors are frequent ("Cold Waste", "The Wandering", "The Fall", "Days of Nothing"). The song "Last Minute Train" has a ballad-like structure. The drumming is decent but non-spectacular as in any album that lacks much dynamism. I have listened to this album for many times and the only catchy song is the more upbeat "The Departure". The only song that doesn't follow the same gothic-doom metal pattern with stylistic differences is "Into the Lips of the Earth", which is a minimalist ambient. 

Lyrically, the album deals with an imaginary apocalypse, the "opera" of an insane man that is fed up with the world. Some monologue can be found in "Ladykiller" and "Last Minute Train". The album cover is well realized and it's related to the theme (man in despair, apocalyptic red sky, ravens). To get the best album experience, you must listen to it from start to finish and follow the lyrics. Everything is good, but there are no standout songs.  

"The Foreshadowing aim is to bring you into an atom-sphere of apocalyptic tragedy and alienation from humanity and everyday life with a moody and powerful music."

That's a quote from one of their official internet pages and i think they transposed their ideas really well into this album. "Days of Nothing" is with nothing inferior to works of more well-known bands such as My Dying Bride, Paradise Lost, Moonspell or Anathema. I really hope the second album won't disappoint my now big expectations.

The Ruins of Beverast is one of the greatest works that could be conceived on this planet. Alexander von Meilenwald is not just any musician, he is someone who seems to belong to another planet.

 The Ruins of Beverast has a philosophy which is "Atmosphere First." This type of music is to make you travel, to immerse yourself in another world, since everything is about the atmosphere that it manages to create and black metal is a genre that fits perfectly with that. Exuvia is delighted with this, absolutely full of nuances that emanate mist, cold and images. It all begins with a recitation of warrior dance, probably by Native Americans, so that after a second of silence the hypnotic arrangements of The Ruins of Beverast begin to resonate. The power begins to develop slowly until all the powerful sound makes its presence. The opening and namesake track is a great piece, no doubt about that. But it is only on the second track called "Surtur Barbaar Maritime" that the wild side of this artist begins. Explosive piece with subdued moments and rather melancholic guitar arrangements, the heavy atmosphere is overwhelming.

It is impossible to deny that Alexander is a master in creating atmosphere, since so far with this album he has shown that it is his specialty, it is an art that he handles without any complications, although that has already been demonstrated since his first album. And suddenly, with a strident and dark introduction, Maere (On a Stillbirth's Tomb) begins, probably the most shabby and dark theme of the album, although the psychedelic atmosphere does not disappear in the least and not to mention the majestic choirs. Then "The Pythia's Pale Wolves" resounds, which attracted my attention mainly because it reminded me of "Rain upon the Impure" as it has a certain similarity. The recitations of the warrior dance return to be coupled with a successive sample of ambient guitar tunes, which near the end that created environment functions as a trigger for the crushing rain of fury that concludes the song. Then "Towards Malakia" and "Takitum Tootem" make an appearance, both can be complemented as a single song, the first has a more hypnotic and emotional atmosphere, while the second presents a more suggestive and dark atmosphere, and also has several experimental sections that add that unpredictable and gloomy touch to it. This album is an authentic ode to introspection, you enter a trance state that prepares us for the next fight.

I have talked a lot about the album in question and everything seems to be going well, but in the end, The Ruins of Beverast, is not the same as before. The fact that it has evolved is undeniable, without betraying the idea that everything must revolve around the atmosphere. However Exuvia is not exactly something truly great on the part of Alexander. While this change started with Foulest Semen of a Sheltered Elite, Exuvia shows a slight return to that formula. Blood Vaults also has a similar sound but is much more forceful, powerful and engaging.

Exuvia is undoubtedly a great album, but it is not at all close to the best that this man did, although it sounds somewhat unfair because everyone knows how utopian it would be to overcome something like Rain upon the Impure, but they do know that if he could overcome or such time to do a job on the same level as Blood Vaults. Exuvia was a bittersweet experience for me, but I still enjoyed it a lot. In any case, The Ruins of Beverast remains one of the projects that I will cherish the most in my entire life.

Arð is the solo doom metal project of Winterfylleth's keyboard player Mark Deeks with contributions from two or three guests, including Atavist drummer Callum Cox behind the kit. In similar vein to Winterfylleth, Arð is thematically linked with Old English history and folklore, in particular the history of the old kingdom of Northumbria, the region of England from which Deeks hails. The band's 2022 debut, Take Up My Bones, related the tale of the journey to find a new resting place for the remains of early english christian saint Cuthbert after the sack of Lindisfarne, with this latest offering focussing on the warrior king Oswald whose conquests laid the foundation for the formation of the Kingdom of Northumbria.

Musically, Untouched by Fire very much picks up where the debut left off, with a version of doom metal that Deeks himself has labelled "monastic doom". This manifests itself as a particularly melodic and atmospheric version of the genre featuring layered vocals that give the impression of monastic choral singing with Wolcensman mainman and former Winterfylleth guitarist Dan Capp providing backing for Deeks. Synths are used extensively, somewhat unsurprisingly given Deeks' day job, draping the riffs with a blanket of wistful atmospherics, redolent with nostalgia for an age long-passed. A pronounced level of introspective spirituality is added by the inclusion of several gentle passages variously using acoustic guitar, piano and cello, which is provided by guest Robina Huy who has previously worked with german symphonic metallers Empyrium. These serene moments, coupled with the chant-like vocals and swelling synths actually provide a positive, almost spiritually uplifting, listening experience.

The tempo is generally pretty slow and whilst not quite as sluggish as you would find in funeral doom, it definitely swims in similar waters and the overall vibe often hints at the approach to funeral doom practiced by several modern acolytes of the sub-genre such as fellow Winterfylleth member Chris Naughton's Atavist. Overall, if you are looking for something that departs from the pack and whose uplifting nostalgia provides a refreshingly different experience from the usual crushing heaviness associated with doom metal, then I would strongly recommend you lend Untouched by Fire your ear.

album: Atomic Carnage in the Temple of Nuclear Hell
texto:
Released under the banner of the Italian record label Despise the Sun Records, Blasphemophagher’s “Atomic Carnage in the Temple of Nuclear Hell” offers a blistering compilation of raw and furious tracks that embody the unhinged energy of war-themed bestial black metal. Pressed way back in 2011, the compendium features tunes pulled from the band’s earlier demos, live recordings, and split albums, showcasing the evolution of their sonic devastation. For fans of their previous works, this corpus brings together some of their most chaotic early offerings with unrelenting intensity.

Several materials on this miscellanea originally appeared in various demos and EPs. The opening ‘Nuclear Storm‘ is an introduction of short duration that sets the apocalyptic tone for the record. This opening, along with the tunes ‘Underskin Blood Implosion‘ and ‘Atomic Infested Carnage‘ were all initially found on the band’s “Atomic Infested Carnage” demo from 2003, where their unrefined lo-fi sound already hinted at the crushing chaos to come in their later works. Those mentioned materials here retain their original fury but are now housed within the larger apocalyptic vision of the selection.

The vile ‘The Return of Bestial Vomit’, which first appeared on the same mentioned first demo above and also came out on their debut “Nuclear Empire of Apocalypse” album in 2008, also finds its way to the track listing of this anthology. This one is recognized for its grinding riffs that helped define the band’s early reputation for audial terror. ‘Cacophonic Death Metal Terrorism‘, which also came out originally from the first rehearsal and was tagged as being one of their standout tracks from earlier releases, was also listed in this recording. This hymn of apocalyptic overture retained the same blend of thrash and death metal riffs it had into a maelstrom of aggressive inharmoniousness as it did with its original version.

Notably, the compilation also includes covers of legendary extreme metal bands such as Sarcófago, Blasphemy, and Beherit, where Blasphemophagher showcased their ability to channel their influences while maintaining their own atrocious edge. These covers are transformed by the trio into venomous and nuclear-fueled renditions that feel both reverential and destructive.

The live tracks on “Atomic Carnage in the Temple of Nuclear Hell” also include pieces like ‘Crawling Nuclear Chaos‘ and ‘Quantum Sphere Annihilation,’ which offer glimpses of their demo and rehearsal origins. Both of these chants of destruction were originally included in the project’s “Nuclear Hell Live – Destroying Rome” live demo. The unfiltered recordings of these live songs deliver a chaotic and raw atmosphere, immersing the listeners in a vortex of cacophonous fury, akin to being in the midst of an atomic explosion.

In the end, “Atomic Carnage in the Temple of Nuclear Hell” is not just a compilation but a demonstration of Blasphemophagher’s adherence to the unrestrained and primal nature of the black/death metal underground. From early demos to their homage to iconic influences, this album brings together the band’s barbarity and tumultuous energy in one bestial package.

album: In Worship Our Blood Is Buried
texto:
"In Worship Our Blood Is Buried" is the debut album of Embryonic Slumber, however the band members, V-KhaoZ and Hellwind Inferion, are well-known persons in the Finnish black metal scene for their other bands, so Embryonic Slumber is not a newcomer in the true sense of the word to many of you. In the press release, "In Worship Our Blood Is Buried" is defined as cosmic black metal – the Embryonic Slumber music is indeed full of cosmic sounds that generate a cold ASMR atmosphere, but if you don't want "to multiply entities without necessity", you can accept that the genre of this album is atmospheric black metal, it's not bad too. 

But there is no denying the truth that atmospheric black metal from Embryonic Slumber is quite unusual. To begin with, blast beats are nowhere to be found on "In Worship Our Blood Is Buried", there is no fast paced drumming here at all. Well, Embryonic Slumber, these Finnish warriors, offer very slow black metal, almost on the verge of depressive black metal. "Almost", but not at all "depressive": firstly, there is no self-pity and feeling of despair in the atmosphere of this work, and secondly, the high pitched shrieking vocals are still not hysterical enough to be an element of depressive black metal (by the way, there are a lot of vocals on "In Worship Our Blood Is Buried"). So it is just very slow atmospheric black metal. 

But this is not the whole story. The fact is that the listener must wait for this atmospheric black metal – songs speed up (if such a word is generally acceptable for Embryonic Slumber) for a very, very long time. It is like a walking meditation under zero gravity. Of the six tracks on the album, two are short – the first, "Intro - Blood, Dust and Twelve Thrones", and the third, "Seven Streams of Sidonay". In these compositions we are dealing with pure black metal ambient, this is a classic of the genre, something in the vein of "Nindinugga Nimshimshargal Enlillara" (1994) by Equimanthorn, just technically more modern (of course, so many years have passed). The last track, "I Am the Storm", also belongs to the category of "short" ones, but we will talk about it later, well, it deserves special attention. 

So now we are talking about three tracks: "Unwavering Flame", "Mortify Your Servant" and "An Oath of Devotion". They demonstrate a unique style of the band in its entirety, these songs are the real Embryonic Slumber, while the rest of the tracks are attracted as a bonus, just for quantity, for the sake of variety, to make the atmosphere more corpulent and so on. Each of these three songs is about 10 minutes long, and they are all built on the same scheme. The first phase: a low humming sound, some gurgling, sighing and groan, plus various cosmic sounds. The second phase: a monotonous melodic line invades this euphonic chaos, it is guitar tremolo picking or guitar plucking or keyboards – sometimes, due to the abundance of sounds, it is impossible to understand what exactly it is. 

As a rule, this melodic line is so monotonous that it gradually turns into just another ambient sound for the listener. Well, the second guitar adds variety to this mesmerizing attack with either segmental chord strumming, or with tremolo picking melody line, however, the second guitar is still the same minimalist, so there is no need to talk about any sophistication. In addiction, very often this phase is accompanied by otherworldly voices or by a declamation with a clean voice. In general, it is safe to say that a full-fledged metal section is preceded by a long ambient part (i. e. the second phase). Such a long preparation leads to the fact that the suspense is constantly growing during the first half of the song – something deep in space intrigues and teases. 

"An Oath of Devotion" is the only song in which the drums come in almost at the very beginning, but these drums are not "true", so to speak, – it is some Indian-tinged ritualistic drum pattern, so it is just an atmospheric decoration. The drum part, as a rule, begins on "In Worship Our Blood Is Buried" with pulsating fills and breaks or floor tom drumming, and after that you have to wait a very long time for a full drum part, with which the main body of the song (or, in our terms, the third phase) begins: in the end, we have that "Unwavering Flame" "starts" from 4:12, "Mortify Your Servant" – from 3:26, and "An Oath of Devotion" – from 3:10. The canonical doublebass-attacks endow the songs with almost aggressive dynamics and mark the culmination of the third phase: "Unwavering Flame" – 4:55, "Mortify Your Servant" – 7:44 (concerning dynamics, it is like a tap is turned on here), "An Oath of Devotion" – 4:29. 

Further, in each drum part, there is an abrupt stop or fade-out, so an ambient piece is formed again, at which the main guitar also most often takes a break. After such a pause, the song returns as if with a vengeance – this illusion arises due to the fact that this time, there is no deliberate procrastination in song progression. There are several such pauses in every song, however, discretion does not arise, partly owing to the strengthening agent, i. e. bass – very low, plangent, and herewith tuneful. The songs also end gradually – the instruments stop playing in turn. Right, in reverse order compared to the beginning, so every time we go back to where we started – ambient. 

As a rule, in the third phase of the composition, some kind of solo appears – a guitar lick or keyboard part. Well, it is not easy to perform solo in such sonic variety, nevertheless, it happens. This effect is especially noticeable in "Mortify Your Servant": at about 5:00 there is a feeling that a tremolo-picked riff sounds in the background, but gradually it becomes louder, louder, louder, so it shoves the keyboards into the shadow, and even drowns out the vocals. 

This one shot underlines the principle on which the album is built: when listening to "In Worship Our Blood Is Buried", it often feels like keyboards and guitars are competing with each other, as if they are trying to squash each other. But this is not a disadvantage at all, the result of this "struggle" is very impressive: a real cosmic attack is underway (well, let's keep quiet about anti-cosmic satanism), you are literally drowning in this sea of noises and sounds. And all this is quite melodic, with a fair amount of despair. Yes, on the verge of depression. In this regard, by the way, "Mortify Your Servant" is very reminiscent of the early works of Burzum: first with a monotonous guitar plucking, and then with a keyboard part. 

All this is very good and even original, but, alas, the sixth song "I Am the Storm" is a real fly in the ointment. This composition is made in an EBM style, or techno or electro-industrial or whatever. Something in the vein of Beherit (some choice pieces, more specifically, from "Electric Doom Synthesis"), Diabolos Rising, Raism, and from modern examples – King Satan. Despite the almost black metal-ish vocals and guitar (judging by the finale), "I Am the Storm" sounds completely off-topic with the previous songs. All the sources stipulate that "I Am the Storm" is exactly a bonus, that is, it has nothing to do with the concept of the album. Nevertheless, it would be better if this track was not included in the album at all. "I Am the Storm" spoils the feeling of the whole album very much. Well, after listening to "In Worship Our Blood Is Buried", you might be wondering "where am I?" or "what happened to my consciousness?" but instead you ask "wtf is this?" The best solution for "I Am the Storm" would be to take it out into a separate project. 

The Metal Observer

I've found this project thanks to the "Similar artists" section in YouTube Music. Although not an expert in DSBM, I am familiar with the more and less common traits of the genre, and I can say that despite not being innovative or outstanding, "Wo Trauer niemals endet" is a pretty strong EP that is worth listening if you are already familiar with the most famous DSBM artists.

There are a few reasons for why I like this album. The first one is its production. While many DSBM artists have a raw sound, "Wo Trauer niemals endet" has a much cleaner one, which is what I normally prefer in all subgenres of metal. The guitar tuning reminds me of Dark Funeral and late Nocturnal Depression, so if you like these bands, you will probably enjoy the guitars here, too. Second of all, the guitar riffs in "Death Addiction", "I Left This Life to Rot", and "Als all Licht meinen Lieb verließ" are absolutely sick (the intros of all the three songs are now among my favorite ones in DSBM). The drumming is decent, especially the awesome blast beat at the beginning of "I Left This Life to Rot". The EP is not long and has no filler songs, making even the extremely conventional intro less annoying and more appropriate than it would be in a lengthier record. The vocals, balancing between evil rattling screaming and melancholic whisper, although not extraordinary in any way, are satisfying and fit the album's desperate atmosphere perfectly. The only arguable song on the album is "Todeslust", where the vocals are in the left channel only, the guitar sometimes sounds a bit awkward (and produces a less "thick" sound), the main riff is way less remarkable and the song length is in my opinion greater than necessary. However, it's not too bad to change my impression of this album greatly.

So, while "Wo Trauer niemals endet" is far from perfect and definitely not the best record to start listening to depressive black metal, those already familiar with the genre will probably find a couple of songs to enjoy in it. A solid album with good songs, pleasing melodies and melancholic atmosphere. Definitely recommended to all DSBM fans, especially those looking for relatively unknown bands with good production.

Static Garden is a bizarre music entity based somewhere in Kentucky. With characters like Jesusatan and Bakhon playing self-described 'Sludgehammer of Eerie Doomtorture', I had to give the music a listen. Bracing myself for laughable and horrible music, I dove into the demo.

About four minutes into the first track "Negroid Sphere of Spectral Darknesses", I suddenly realized that this doesn't suck. How can a single guitar and drum kit sound so dense? The music is oddly alluring. Riffage is rather nice and thankfully there is more than one to a song. The high-pitched angry intro riff of "Negroid Sphere" along with the screeched vocals and real drums work in creating a dark atmosphere that I was unprepared for. It's not exactly funeral doom since it lacks the molasses feel that genre is famous for, and the music has a strong affinity to black metal. That said, this release is almost all andante or moderato and could pass as funeral doom to the uninformed ear. Over the course of the songs (bar Transylvanian Virgin), the riffs mutate smoothly, each transformation meaner than the last. There are a few slip ups occasionally performance-wise, but nothing drastic enough to break the listener's concentration or the mood. The vocals are by all means suitable and are a main component behind the "evil and deranged" factor this demo has going. Jesusatan alternates between angry shouts, piercing wails, and cracking screams. There's a lot of power behind the singing and taking into account the vocalist's supposed young age, it's quite a feat.

Transylvanian Virgin is a strange piece. All it really is is sloppy drumming over a one note riff with random wailing. This is the definite low point of the demo because it's uninteresting and hard to make sense of. It is understandable how some listeners could find it charming or anti-innovative in an innovative way, but I believe the vast majority will find themselves skipping over, or at least through, this track. This isn't too much of a downfall since the song clocks in at just over six and a half minutes, less than an eighth of the total runtime. 

Next up is the massive closing track. It's apparent after the intro that Silent Dive is very inappropriately named. The first half proceeds at a moderately slow tempo, incorporating a plodding, slightly dissonant, and ever-changing riff that somehow retains its identity. This is followed by a thoroughly black metal riff. It promptly falls apart layer by layer impressively amongst scattered drum fills and tortured shouts, yielding to a wild seven minute guitar solo that ends the song. It sure is ambitious in scope and somehow manages to fulfill it's purpose. The listener feels as though s/he is being violently dragged along, resisting, until his/her strength ebbs and is pulled down through Hell and beyond.

Though this is a raw demo and it sounds like it was recorded in a garage, it turned out great for what it is. There are no silly "torture" samples, rattling chains, or other unintentionally amusing sounds (nor does the vocalist wallow for minutes, screaming his lungs out senselessly). It should also be noted here that even though this was recorded "live" through the air, the instruments are clear and none threaten to overpower another.  While the songs do have an average length of about 10 minutes, they don't get stuck in the same rut that many funeral doom bands do. That is, the riffs are not repeated until the listener simply cannot stand them anymore. I've skimmed over this band's later material and I must say that I like this release the best. Curious fans of doom and black metal should grab a copy and take a stroll through the Static Garden.

Man, I was not expecting this! Strapping Young Land and Godlesh both ended, Nailbomb showed no sign of a follow up, and Fear Factory completely mellowed out. Industrial metal had pretty much ended before it had even begun, and I was pretty sure we wouldn't get any more great albums in that style.

So of course, after the first few moments of 'Deadline' I could not have been more surprised. The album wasn't even thirty seconds in and I had already had my ass kicked through the roof! This is some seriously brutal stuff. Ground Zero play hard, sickeningly repetitive industrial mixed with groove and death metal influences, and the end result couldn't be heavier! Just take the opening track for instance - after perhaps 20 seconds of ambience the listener is all of a sudden slammed to the floor by a super fast, repetitive industrial chug, a rhythm which could drive a man mad if it wasn't broken up with a simple (but good) groove metal riff for the chorus section. The production is clear and heavy, the vocals are powerful (whether growled with hatred or moaned and sung cleanly) and the playing is super tight. All signs of a great band, it just so happens that Ground Zero also happen to be really great songwriters, making 'Deadline' one of the most brutal albums of 2009 so far.

I should say that this is a loooooong album, over an hour long, and a lot of the music here is super repetitive. But I wouldn't have it any other way. Ground Zero play an excellent mix of industrial and groove metal, and both genres rely fully on repetition. Usually you'll have one really simplistic yet addictive brutal chugged riff repeating over and over until you can barely handle it anymore, and then finally you get a good chorus hook just to prepare you for another onslaught of groovy, industrial madness. Did I mention that this album is ridiculously heavy? It sounds like it was played by T200s as a warning of how they would later dominate the earth. Seriously, the music here must have been written by homicidal machines, it's so hateful and relentless that there's no way anything with a soul could have partaken in the creation of it (except perhaps the beautiful more emotional songs 'Story of Sadness' and 'The Noises in My Head', but even those are more cold than soulful). 

This should be taken up my a big label immediately and have thousands of copies pressed, there's absolutely no reason that this should be a self-released demo. Any fans of seriously brutal music should check this out, aswell as anyone that wishes that industrial metal had lasted a little longer. Ground Zero do not disappoint.

Much has already been written about bands who figure things out as they go. A shaky but promising first release, a minor change in sound in a spare demo or EP, and boom, a new record that showcases the direction that was previously hinted upon in a fully realised manner, which is then met with praise or derision by critics and fanbase. Tale as old as time. While there are many who are content simply refining their sound over the course of their career, I find the aforementioned approach to be far more interesting to observe as a reviewer and music fan. Really, that’s what makes Nihilism’s sophomore, Cataclysme vers l’Ascendance so fascinating to me, because not only does it give us something entirely different to what preceded it, it came about in the span of a mere two years, during which the band was radio silent.

From the moment “I” breaks out, you’d almost be forgiven for thinking an entirely different band worked on this. Gone is the prolonged introduction, we’re immediately met with cacophonous blasting and ringing dissonant notes that possess a near-mathy character. Hell, even Chris Bonos seems to have found his place, his previously shy screeching at the front, injected with a much needed shot of adrenaline. Sure, Obscurite Noir wasn’t necessarily lacking in intensity, but it was nowhere near as lively. The choppy riffing presented here is equal parts brain-bending and pummelling, and things remain unpredictable throughout the song’s 4 minute length. It’s genuinely astounding how much they manage to cram in without losing the plot. Music this shifty requires everyone involved to be in lockstep, not only in terms of playing, but also in terms of vision. I hate to repeatedly draw comparisons to previous works in my reviews, but I really can’t wrap my head around how they managed to invert their writing approach of “3 minutes’ worth of ideas stretched to 5”, and keep it cohesive.

“II” sees the duo further spread their wings, with a slightly greater emphasis on atmosphere, without necessarily sacrificing intensity. Wrenching grooves are offset by rampant percussion coursing underneath them, the slight disagreement in tempo keeping the listener guessing, while also giving them a trail to follow. The whole thing is a roller coaster really, as Nihilism also manages to inject some slower parts into the mix without robbing the piece of its tension. Guitar breaks uphold an equilibrium of tension and tranquillity, and always escalate towards something, be it one of the band’s majestic tremolo streams, or a lopsided arpeggiated groove. Radical as their transformation might have been, the fact that they knew what they should keep from the debut is reassuring, as the aforementioned tremolos do a lot to help mix things up, in addition to providing a foil to the discordant jangling that permeates the music.

Unfortunately, it doesn’t take long for things to start feeling more and more scatterbrained. “III” is a dour and sludgy instrumental, that, despite its quality, comes much too early in the album and kneecaps the momentum that was built up to that point, and after all my listens, I am not quite sure if it ever manages to recover from that. The album begins to move in fits and starts, more akin to a sputtering car engine than a black metal onslaught, “IV” also featuring brass and choir breaks alongside the bursts of dissonant black metal. Cataclysme vers l’Ascendance makes an attempt to course-correct through that song, but things come to a screeching halt IMMEDIATELY AFTER with “V”, an ambient composition that contents itself with droning and groaning around for longer than it has any business to. I understand that an element of the avant-garde is unpredictability, but given that we’re talking about a conceptual work, especially one that lasts a mere 34 minutes, it’s hard not to feel the whiplash from one moment to the next.

Even though the last third of Cataclysme vers l’Ascendance manages to bring things back with “VI”’s labyrinthine and grandiose finale (awkward clean vocals included), and a denouement that actually means something in “VII”, with its female-vocal driven post-cataclysmic bliss, it doesn’t pass muster. It’s the equivalent of plummeting down a cliff and having your fall interrupted multiple times over by stopping on another cliff and needing someone to push you so that you can keep going down. In brief, the density of ideas per song is pretty solid, but when you take a wider lens to look at the entirety of the album it falls out of whack because it’s doing too much on a track-by-track basis. Sure, the concept of “an apocalypse brings about a new world that allows us to transcend” is there, but it feels like I’m watching it unfold at x2 speed, and it deserves better than feeling like a sped-up YouTube video.

Ironically enough, it feels like Nihilism were tempering their ambitions on this one. Cataclysme vers l’Ascendance is beholden to the same constraints their debut was in terms of its duration and track listing, when in reality its leaps in style and technique deserved so much more. Looking at individual parts under a microscope shows us a band that has fully come into its own, creating erratic and contorting music that suffocates and elevates the listener in equal measure, but I can’t help but feel like they don’t let us absorb the vistas we see in the journey they created. Even then, despite its hectic nature, it continues to be a commendable effort, and a bold step forward for what had started as a merely vicious black metal band with little else to help it stand out. I can only hope we get to see something new from them in the future, perhaps another great leap forward, one that actually gets the time it deserves.

Angel Sword's debut Rebels Beyond the Pale was a diamond-studded masterpiece, blustering onto the scene with the oft claimed and seldom delivered boast that they sounded like an 80's metal band. They did the unthinkable by not only penning an authentic treatise on the subject, but in an astoundingly unique way. Vocal harmonies sounded like a barbershop quartet of biker demons, guitar solos gushed with emotion despite their inherent simplicity; it was like Motörhead and Manilla Road wedded in unholy matrimony. Could Neon City possibly improve upon this formula?

...I personally don't think so, but keep in mind I'm a helplessly addicted speed freak. Try as I might, I never found Neon City quite as captivating as Rebels Beyond the Pale, due primarily to its more weighty, pensive approach to songwriting. Sure, there are a few hot tamales like 'Evil Eye' thrown in, but overall this album seems a bit shy to flex their muscles anywhere but their own mirror. I think Cirith Ungol's One Foot in Hell is an apt comparison, though one that fails to paint the complete picture due to the friggin' werewolf behind the microphone.

Jerry Razors is a baritone beast as always: there's so much grizzled machismo in his voice, I can almost smell the bacon on his breath. It's a raspy howl that may at first may seem a bit austere and one-dimensional, but the notes he's able to reach and harmonies he's able to effectively spearhead sound like Solid Snake after opera lessons. 'Starlight Shadow' begins with a fairly humdrum bass-driven gallop, though it's quickly dominated by dazzlingly high alto registers from Jerry. Before you know it, he's delved into an aphotic baritone that reaches lower pitches than most locomotive engines.

This infernal bellow leads the charge for most every layered chorus; a technique strikingly similar to what's used throughout Heavy Load's Stronger than Evil, not to mention countless unsung USPM greats like Glacier's self-titled EP. But for those of us who have shamelessly air guitared to 'Run with the Devil' or 'Devil in Disguise' (that was unintentional), you may be a bit disappointed to find how inert Neon City can seem sometimes. (Get it? Because neon is an inert gas. That one was intentional). 

This goes back to my previous point: It's clear Angel Sword have a real knack for enchanting melodies far more effusive and emotional than they have any right to be. It seems to me they have intentionally distanced themselves from bloodthirsty speed metal in order to explore the full potential of these slower, artsier avenues. Which may remind you, almost uncertainly unfavorably, of Enforcer's Zenith. The moseying harmonies of Neon City feels significantly less contrived than Zenith, yet in a contextual sense, the similarity is almost uncanny. If you yearned for another high voltage onslaught like Rebels Beyond the Pale could offer you with 'Lords of Thunder' or 'Lightning Runners', you may be a teensy bit underwhelmed by the mid-tempo grooves of Neon City.

However, these grooves are still tremendously well-written, and the caked-on mood and atmosphere are very much carried over from previous affairs. If it seemed like I was unusually hard on this album, it's only because Rebels Beyond the Pale was such a goddamn masterpiece. You should listen to it, you should listen to this album too, and you should ignore how abruptly this review ends.

Katatonia is my favorite band and it’s always fun to examine their releases in depth. 1993’s “Dance of December Souls” is the band’s debut, a raw piece of music somewhere between death/doom metal and black/doom metal. It’s a highly regarded and influential album in both subgenres.

At this point, Katatonia was a band that relied a lot on its youthful vigor and passion. The sorrow on “Dance of December Souls” is extremely apparent in every aspect, from the heartwrenching guitar melodies to Jonas Renkse’s tortured screams. Masterminds Jonas and Anders were not even in their 20's at this point and do their best to create a dismal feeling of sorrow.

And Katatonia certainly succeeds. After a short intro, the album opens up with “Gateways of Bereavement”, which goes for the throat right away. Slow, brooding power chords linger and support the vocals. Jonas screams his guts out, and with this approach it’s not surprising that his voice couldn’t take extreme vocals in the long run. Much of the music is what became Scandinavian extreme doom metal; a mix of early melodic death metal sounds and the heaviness from traditional-sounding doom metal.

The Scandinavian scene was arguably at its most creative at this point, forming genre blueprints still valid to this day. "Dance of December Souls" is extremely important in that sense. Just like 1996's "Brave Murder Day", this laid down many foundations for future death/doom metal bands. I believe this album was also very instrumental in shaping the more depressive forms of black metal. The way Jonas spews out the lyric lines on this album reminds me quite a lot of what was to come in the more negative forms of black metal.

But beyond its importance, how does this fit into the Katatonia discography? Well, it certainly has many recognizable traits. A Katatonia trademark already present on “Dance of December Souls” are the guitar melodies. Just like on most of their material, there are many guitar moves that are as memorable and emotional as they are simple. “Without God” and “In Silence Enshrined” have especially brilliant lines.

It really is the guitars that drive everything on this album. The mood and execution of the guitars range from darkly nihilistic to absolutely dreamy. The strong shoegaze influences hadn't quite become a part of their sound yet, but there are some very moody acoustic and clean guitar sections on here. Frontman Jonas Renkse plays the drums, and as a result the beats are extremely simple and mere support to the guitars.

However, an album as youthful and passionate is almost bound to have its downsides. And it does. Some of the compositions are massive and not that fluently written. There are many epic sections and shifts between distorted and clean guitars. Some of the transitions are not particularly smooth. The shorter songs, like “Without God”, feel more fluent and compact. It stands in strong contrast to Katatonia’s clean vocal material where the songwriting is central and absolutely meticulous.

There are also some stylistic jumps that don't mold all too well. The album has traces of death metal, black metal, doom metal and even traditional metal. Sometimes it sounds angry, sometimes dreamy, sometimes almost triumphant. There's not really enough consistency, beyond the main objective of being very depressive. I think the ambitions were simply set a bit too high, considering how new Katatonia was at the time.

Despite its flaws, it’s hard to overstate how important this album is for the extreme side of the doom metal genre. It paved the way for death/doom and later developments like depressive black metal and blackgaze. It’s my least favorite full-length from my favorite band, but still a damn solid piece of early death/doom metal. I am very impressed by how they could achieve something like this so early. You can already tell that Katatonia was going places.

Listening to this album, I expected Ethereal Shroud to be a group of at least three members but to my (very pleasant) surprise ES turns out to be the solo project of one Joe Hawker. For a second album, "They Became the Falling Ash" is a stupendous effort in layered atmospheric depressive blackened doom metal. It has many elements that should make it a great album: a distinctive ghostly ambience that heightens the moods and emotions expressed in the songs; a firm grasp of the types of melodies, riffs and sounds that produce an impending feeling of chaos and hysteria; good use of reverb and other effects; and a style and production that make the music monstrous. It does fall short of being great, and that's a pity - but it's better to strive for greatness, to approach making recordings as if each and every one of them is going to be your last and the only legacy of yours that you leave behind.

All three tracks on this album weigh in at a minimum 10 minutes and two of them reach beyond the 24-minute mark so you have some idea of the heights Hawker has turned his target sights towards. First track "Look Upon the Light" sets the tone for the rest of the recording to follow: it's a roller-coaster ride over hills and through dales of intense heightened emotion, shrill trilling tremolo guitars heralding the way, raging storms of bass grind, percussion ranging from blast-beat super-fast to emphatic crashes, and in the far background gruff crunching-rock vocals growling through lyrics of mass fiery ritual sacrifices. While this is a ginormous epic piece of dense layered guitar-distortion grind, I'd have liked the singing and the lyrics to be clearer, as the imagery in them is so vivid and worth emphasising in their own right. 

"Desperation Hymn" is not much more than an extension of the first track and again the vocals are deeply buried in murky reverb. Being squinched between two monster pieces, both of which bleed into it, and not having much of an identity of its own, this song deserves a different treatment to work as an effective interlude: a sharper sound, less reverberation and a bit less bombast perhaps.

"Echoes in the Snow" is a more melancholic and elegiac doom piece, and there is greater emphasis on melody and less on dense textured fierce tremolo guitar battery. Emotion is much more complex and expressive here. As with the previous two songs, the singing is shrouded in too much reverb though given the song's subject matter and its place in what is essentially a trilogy of songs, the vocals should be very wraith-like. The song's resolution is handled very gradually and delicately as death claims its victims and disperses their material being into dust. After the arduous journey through existential torment, the peace that follows when the album ends is serene indeed.

The whole album is hard-hitting and can be an exhausting experience over one hour but it does need to be heard in one sitting to be fully appreciated for what it is. The twists and turns and the laborious journey from one climax to the next in all three tracks trace the transition experienced as one passes from life through ritual sacrifice to death and dissolution, and the interrogation with God that takes place during that transition. I really would have liked a bit more variation in the instrumentation during the long extended instrumental passages - maybe a cello in one track, more piano in another - to contrast against the guitars-and-drums juggernaut delivery.

Even with its shortcomings, this is a well-crafted opus that deserves a reissue (with the sound cleaned up a bit and the vocals brought further up in the mix) on a specialist BM or doom metal label.

Continuing the unofficial series of albums and bands I liked in 2003 - Valley of the Damned. I discovered this album back in the days of MP3.com (I actually think that was before the release of the album), and it was this, Shadowland by Nocturnal Rites and Evilized by Dream Evil. But this was my favorite. And I told all my friends about it. Ironic that this band would arguably become one of the most visible pure power metal bands in the world. Up to this point my only real exposure to metal was Slayer, Iron Maiden and Megadeth. Dragonforce stood out to me for playing melodic music at a blistering pace. The blazing pace and noodling guitars really separated it from stuff like Iron Maiden.

Silly memories aside, this album really has it's upside, and the majority of tracks stand the test of time. Looking back even today, I cannot firmly nail down who exactly their influences are. The quickness of the drum beats, the tremolo picking, guitar harmonization and noodly leads, and the choir vocals that sometimes harmonize. Other than their countrymen, Powerquest, who debuted right around the same time, I can't see where their influence comes from. And even still Powerquest aren't this over-the-top. Sure, Judas Priest had the harmonized guitar leads, and Queen had harmonized vocals. But that hardly accounts for their whole sound.

The production quality of this album really reminds me of early Blind Guardian, it's nice and unpolished. It actually sounds like dudes playing instruments, not a product made in a lab (which is funny considering how terrible they were live). It still has a touch of a "demo"-y quality, but it really allows for dynamics and the sound of real playing. It's great. I wish every album had this quality. Within the mix the vocals even have a bit of live feel, and ZP's performance is just fantastic, with all the poise and power that you need for this style.

Back then, the most remarkable thing about this album - and still to most people today, I'm sure - is their speed and oodles of guitar noodles. But listening now, the thing that stands out the most is the vocal harmonies and song structures. Many, many bands do the standard power metal things: fast drums, quick melodic guitar leads and high, powerful vocals, but actually using vocal harmonies and backup vocals throughout is fairly uncommon. It gives it so much more sonic depth, it's just very pleasing to the ear, as silly as that seems to say. The keyboards are also used really well to complement the vocals.

The song structures are kind of like if you took a normal song and split it in half and wedged another song inside of it. In the case of Disciples of Babylon, it's more like a normal 4 minute track that gives  way to a moody flamenco type passage, that evolves further into Latin jazz and folds back in the flamenco, then back into the jazz with a solo. Incredible as it seems, it really works.

A couple tracks are little bit more on the generic side like like Revelations and Black Fire, but are still strong tracks regardless. Both tracks are helped immensely by the aforementioned vocal harmonies. 

Okay, so the album also has it's weak spots. The lyrics are pretty terrible. Having two songs with the word "black" and "fire" within 3 tracks is a serious misstep that has always irked me. Not to mention two tracks with the word "star" - I mean, Jesus, you're British, and you can't think of more than 3 words for your song titles. Starfire is punishingly corny piano ballad. Evening Star is also a weak track, with only the build up to the chorus being very noteworthy. And today, the guitar playing is a lot less impressive and more just style over substance.

Highlights are definitely the title track and Disciples of Babylon. Both have a hint of speed metal, super catchy choruses, and epic song structures. The title track remains an all-time classic power metal song, how much of that is nostalgia I can't say, but it will remain a classic for me.

This album has very high highs, and some very low lows. But the strong tracks ultimately outweigh the weak and make this required listening for any power metal fan.

Right. This was the first SM album I got, having heard only 1 or 2 tracks beforehand. It`s their 3rd album, and at the time of purchase I thought it was great. The best thing to ever come out of japanese metal full stop. Only years later did I get an opportunity to collect the remainder of their catalogue, which then blew me away completely. I had read reviews on the internet that said that BBQ was the best, yet because the superiority of the previous albums was unexpected, it was all the more remarkable. But looking back on it now and listening to it, the 3rd release following an incredible debut and a highly competent 2nd album is actually not bad. At all. It is a high quality album with a few low pointsm that is all. Without those low points it would be just as good as those two albums which are worthy of a place on the international metal classics lists. Let`s look at the tracks. 

1. S.H.R. -Sexy Hero Revolution- - Good energetic opener. For me, nothing too special.

2. Midori No Obachan - A definite high point! An excellent tracks with great lead harmony parts. Melodic, with a catchy chorus and excellent soloing. Song about a lollipop lady (you know the people who stop cars to let you cross the street).

3. Ookami To Kirigirisu - It`s OK I guess but nothing special. A thrash song. Based on the Aesop`s fable about the ants and the locust. Except it`s about a wolf and a locust. And tells of how you`ve gotta act if you aren`t happy about your life.

4. Punch De Love Attack - About asking a girl out. Nice soloing but not the best track on this album.

5. Death - An homage to death metal this does exactly what it says on the tin. Weaker track IMO.

6. Aikoso Subete - Now we`re talking! This is a damn fine thrash song about confessing a love affair to your wife. Good track nice ending too.

7. Pheromones - A song about being attracted to girls by their pheromones. Weak melody, not a bad track. Not a good one either.

8. Touchan - Tribute to Metallica`s Battery! Very similar sounding, not as good (what do you expect?) but great fun nonetheless. About his dad and how he works so hard to support his family. It`s basically a song of thanks.

9. Salaryman Arashi - About a frustrated unmotivated office worker kinda like Kevin Spacey in American Beauty. An average thrash song. 

10. Tabetai Nametai Kikenchitai - A song about eating and about love. Kinda strange. 

11. Fire - Dramatic start and an awesome solo, with some amazong technical sweeps on the guitar by Anchang the lead guitarist and vocalist. Best track here, alongside Midori No Obachan as SM greats.

As you can see from my review, a mixed bag, the good tracks are great, the bad tracks not amazing but tolerable, it`s all a matter of context. If an average japanese thrash band wrote those, then they`d be good. Because it`s SM they don`t seem as good. But still, the good points of this album alone make it worth purchasing. Get the first two albums first.

Over the years, I've managed to review five of Bodom's then-current seven albums (don't read the first four of them, for your sanity's sake).  They're not a band I ever really set out to constantly cover, but when a band is as important to me as this one is/was, and when said band finds itself on such a consistently downwards slide, it's hard not to pipe up every time they disappoint you.  I maintain, even after all these years, that Follow the Reaper is one of the most important albums in my development as a metal fan, helping ease me from the HerPeS-only mindset into more and more extreme metal thanks to my eventual acclimation with Alexi Laiho's frenzied yowling.  The vocals and lyrics have always technically sucked, but the level of enthusiasm was so high that it never mattered.  It fit perfectly and just the sheer amount of fun the band was having with the light melodies and preposterously wanky dueling solos rubbed off on the listener.  That all changed with Are You Dead Yet?, which focused more on heavy chugging and less on guitar/keyboard theatrics and fast paced and fun melodies.  Ever since then, the band has been on the steady decline, releasing three crappy mostly-melodeath albums with wretched lyrics, banal, insipid jokes for cover tracks, and just really lazy songwriting.  Years and years we fans have put up with the band just not giving a single fuck about anything, churning out brainless albums every few years, collecting a paycheck, spending it all on booze, and then making another shitty album to pay for their next supply of booze.

And then 2013 rolls around, and queue in Halo of Blood, the band's eighth album.  Right off the bat, the aesthetics felt kinda different.  The last three (bad) albums had all portrayed Roy in a more straightforward and vicious light, rife with menacing poses and gory splatter, whereas the earlier albums I love so much always seemed to portray the embodiment of death in a more romantic, mysterious light.  Compare the cover for Follow the Reaper, where the Reaper is standing calmly in a graveyard, beckoning you forth, to the cover of Blooddrunk, where he's viciously slashing somebody with blood splattered all over the place.  From "Death be not proud..." to "I DON'T GIVE A FLYING FUCK MOTHERFUCKER!"  Clearly two massively different approaches to both their aesthetics and their music itself.  Halo of Blood rolls around and suddenly it looks much more subdued.  The palette is very predominately white (which could symbolize something lighter than previous, less dark), with the trademark Grim Reaper looking down remorsefully upon a frozen lake; where the snow has been brushed away you can see the water is packed with screaming victims, frozen under the surface.  This is intriguing, this piques my interest.  That romanticized take on death that used to counteract the band's youthful exuberance is so much more interesting than the last three albums which simply reaffirm the band's juvenile nature. 

But moving past that... yeah, the throwback artwork is 100% indicative of the sound to be found on Halo of Blood.  I could not be happier for what this album is, I really couldn't.  The fifteen year old version of myself wet himself with happiness merely two tracks in.  This is the true successor to Hate Crew Deathroll, ten sad years after the fact.  As far as I'm concerned, this album just erased two and a half albums worth of ill will that Bodom had built up.  Relentless Reckless Forever, Blooddrunk, and all but about three-ish songs on Are You Dead Yet? no longer exist to me.  Bodom's drug fueled mishaps of the mid-late 00s were all just some strange hallucinatory fever dream I had.  They never sucked!  Hooray!

The important thing is that the music is good, right?  Well, this album finally one-ups its predecessors by actually doing just that, making good music.  The opening track, "Waste of Skin", utilizes a main melody quite similar to "Hate Me" from the stellar Follow the Reaper, and just revels in this lighthearted melody that the band used to always throw around in abundance.  This is the throwback we've been waiting for, one that came straight from the heart, not the wallet.  This is loaded with tracks that wouldn't sound out of place on the band's third or fourth albums ("Waste of Skin", "Bodom Blue Moon", "One Bottle and a Knee Deep", "All Twisted"), and this is the sound that I and countless other fans have been pining for for roughly ten years now.  I feel like, somewhere down the line, Bodom got a wake up call of sorts.  I'm not sure what or where or how, but the band collectively realized that they just weren't connecting like they used to, and had to think about how to stir up the passion within their fans again. The trick was to just... just try again.  It's clear to me that the band wasn't didn't really have their heart in the last two albums, as they all just seemed to kind of go through the motions.  Halo of Blood feels like the band is pouring themselves into the writing process again.  They're having fun again, and for the first time in years, so am I.

I'm not going to sit here and pretend that there are a wide array of influences at work, but there are indeed a few different moments.  Most notable is the nearly Dissection-esque meloblack influence in the title track, which ranks among the fastest songs the band has ever written.  I'm most pleased with the fact that Bodom went back to doing what they did best, but that doesn't mean I don't also appreciate them trying something new (mostly because it works, as opposed to the last three albums of new ideas).  There are a few bum spots as well, since there are still some minor holdover from the chuggy days with "Damage Beyond Repair".  And yet again we have one of their kinda-trademarked terrible slow songs here in "Dead Man's Hand on You".  Really, does anybody honestly prefer the slow Bodom songs like "Angels Don't Kill" or "Banned from Heaven" over "Towards Dead End" or "Kissing the Shadows"?  If you do, I've got a fiver on you also preferring the doomy Overkill songs, you freak of nature.  The point is that they're an inherently energetic band, so toning it down really doesn't do them any favors.  It's like Stone Cold Steve Austin hosting a cooking show where he never once puts a crowd member through a table or Stone Cold Stunners Rachel Ray, it's a situation wherein the band/host isn't playing to their strengths.  "Scream for Silence" does the same thing, but it's got a better pace and moves along well enough to not be too irritating (though the main melody has a really obviously flat note that seems completely out of place, which is irritating since it repeats so much). 

But with those quibbles aside, there isn't a whole lot I dislike about Halo of Blood.  It's the best kind of reversion I could have ever asked for.  The keys are back in a relatively prominent role (much more so than the fuck all they did on Blooddrunk), ripping through overindulgent solo battles with Laiho's lead guitar just like the old days, along with providing melodies over the verses and such.  "All Twisted" and "One Bottle and a Knee Deep" are great examples of this hearkening back to the glory days.  He still doesn't let loose as much as he does for Warmen, but he does finally get some more opportunities to exercise those wacky spiderfingers of his.  After several, several listens, I still can't tell if the lyrics are as drop dead derpy as they always have been, but to the album's credit, there aren't any titles as fucknards stupid as "Northpole Throwdown" this time around, and I'm not hearing "YOW" at the beginning of every single song nor "FUCK" at every sixth word, so it seems like Laiho has finally, finally learned how to write lyrics.  There's a good possibility I'm wrong though, feel free to point out any horrid examples I may have missed.  Even the cover song is good again.  I mean think about it, early on the band was covering Iron Maiden, Stone, and W.A.S.P., and then around the time they started getting shitty, they started covering Britney Spears, Kenny Rogers, and Eddie Murphy.  Their cover song has always been a good indicator of their attitude at the time, and they morphed from musicians having fun and covering their influences to a bunch of durr hurr lol random Invader Zim dipshits covering anything they thought was funny.  So who do we get this time around?  The mo'fuckin' Thunder in the East, LOUDNESS!  Yeah, "Crazy Nights" is a kind of silly song, but it's silly in how over the top cheesy it is, as opposed to silly in the sense of METAL BAND COVERING POP SONGS?!  OH PSHAW!  They're tackling metal again, and it's awesome.

That melodic death/power metal hybrid I've been missing so much is back in full force, and Bodom fans around the world should rejoice, for the band has finally pulled their collective heads out of each other's collective asses.  This still have a focus on heaviness in parts, as opposed to the "really fast Nightwish songs with ridiculous screechy vocals" of the first two/three albums, so if you didn't like Hate Crew Deathroll, then chances are you won't like Halo of Blood either.  But let me tell you, I (and thousands of other fans) would much rather have a Hate Crew 2: Electric Boogaloo than Blooddrunk 2: Drunk Harder.  Comeback of the year for me, hands down.
